input:
Principle
A heat exchanger is a piece of equipment that passes heat from a hot stream across to a cold stream through a solid wall that keeps the two streams apart. The hot stream leaves colder than it entered, the cold stream leaves warmer, and the heat lost by one stream is essentially the heat gained by the other, apart from losses to the surroundings, which a first treatment normally sets aside. The rate at which the heat is transferred is governed by three quantities in particular: the area of the wall that is available, the temperature difference that exists between the two streams at the place being considered, and an overall heat-transfer coefficient, which bundles the resistances of the two fluid films and of the wall itself into a single number. The temperature difference is by no means constant along the exchanger. Each stream changes temperature as it travels, so the difference between the streams at the inlet end is not the same as at the outlet end, and the local difference at each point along the wall determines the local rate there. What is needed is a mean difference for the exchanger as a whole. Where the overall coefficient and the specific heat capacities of the two streams can be treated as constant along the length, that mean turns out to be the log-mean temperature difference. The flow arrangement also sets the end differences. In countercurrent flow the two streams travel in opposite directions, whereas in cocurrent flow they travel in the same direction and enter together. The example that is used throughout this chapter is a countercurrent exchanger in which a hot stream enters at 160 °C and leaves at 80 °C, and a cold stream enters at 30 °C and leaves at 60 °C.

Equipment
The shell-and-tube exchanger is generally regarded as the standard construction for process duty. One stream flows inside a bundle of tubes while the other flows through the shell around the bundle, crossing the tubes as baffles direct it. The construction takes high pressure and high temperature in its stride, the tube bundle can be withdrawn for cleaning, and individual tubes can be plugged when they fail, without scrapping the unit. The shell-and-tube exchanger is the heavier and more expensive construction per unit of area, and the shell-side stream sees a less uniform flow than the tube-side stream. The plate exchanger, by contrast, is built up from a stack of thin pressed plates, with the two streams flowing in alternate gaps between the plates and with gaskets sealing the edges of the pack. The pack provides a large area in a small volume and turbulence even at low flow, so the coefficients are high and the approach temperatures close. The pack can be opened for cleaning by hand, and plates added or removed to change the duty. The gaskets set the limits of the plate exchanger: the gasket material fixes the highest temperature and the pressure the pack can hold, and aggressive fluids attack the gasket before they attack the plate. The double-pipe exchanger, one pipe inside another, serves smaller duties. The construction is simple, the flow truly countercurrent, and lengths of pipe are added to gain area, but the area per unit is small and the construction becomes clumsy as the duty grows. Fouling governs the maintenance of all three constructions: a stream that deposits on the wall adds a resistance the designer must allow for and the operator must clean away, and the choice between constructions is often a choice about which unit can be cleaned, and at what interval, without stopping the plant around it.

Worked example
This worked example calculates the log-mean temperature difference for the exchanger introduced in the Principle section. The end differences are taken from the stream temperatures stated there, and no new data are introduced. At the end of the exchanger where the hot stream comes in, the hot stream is at 160 °C and the cold stream is leaving at 60 °C, which means that the difference at that particular end comes to 100 K. At the other end, where the hot stream leaves, the hot stream is at 80 °C and the cold stream is entering at 30 °C, so the difference at that end comes to 50 K. The log-mean temperature difference itself is calculated from these two end differences by taking the difference between them and dividing it by the logarithm of the ratio of the two end differences. Working this through gives a value of 72.1 K. A useful check on the result is where the value sits: a mean of the two end differences ought to lie between them, and the log-mean value falls between the larger and the smaller end difference, closer to the smaller, as the form of the mean requires. The area of the exchanger then follows from the duty: dividing the duty by the product of the overall coefficient and the log-mean temperature difference gives the area the exchanger must provide, and a designer who has the duty and the coefficient has the size of the unit from this one calculation.

Limits
The simple model of this chapter rests on conditions that plant exchangers meet only in part, and this section states where the model stops describing the unit in front of the designer. The overall coefficient is treated as constant along the exchanger. Fouling breaks that condition in service: deposits build unevenly, the coefficient falls as the run proceeds, and an exchanger sized exactly on the clean coefficient is undersized before the first cleaning falls due. The specific heat capacities have likewise been treated as constants, which is why each stream temperature has been shown changing in a straight line along the length. A stream whose properties change strongly with temperature will instead tend to follow a curved path, the local difference will depart from the log-mean picture, and the resulting error will grow as the temperature range across the unit increases. The flow has also been treated as though it were purely countercurrent or purely cocurrent. A multipass shell-and-tube unit is, in reality, neither of these things, because the tube-side stream reverses direction and part of its travel is cocurrent with the shell stream, which means that the true mean difference is smaller than the log-mean value for the same end temperatures, so the simple model tends to overstate the driving force and undersize the unit. A stream that undergoes a change of phase will hold its temperature constant while it condenses or boils, and the picture of two sloping temperature lines does not describe such a stream at all. Heat losses to the surroundings have been set aside throughout the chapter, and on a small or poorly lagged unit such a loss is a genuine term in the overall balance, with the heat gained by the cold stream falling short of the heat lost by the hot stream by the amount that has been lost. The model is therefore best understood as a sizing model for a clean, steady, single-phase exchanger, and each departure from those conditions is a departure that the designer needs to price separately.
